source_neutral.procedure: Starting state: a checkout latency regression has been reported, and a deployed change that was present during the regression is suspected. Deployment/configuration history and request traces are used to select one candidate change and to define the affected checkout paths and traffic strata. The candidate's causal role, its independent reversibility, and the safety of experimenting on it are treated as hypotheses to be checked, not as established facts. It is determined whether removing the candidate would also change other revisions, configuration or shared state; if these cannot be separated, the factor under test is the whole rollback bundle and not the single change. Overall process: pre-specify measurement and safety parameters; where independently reversible and safe, remove the candidate from a bounded cohort while a comparable contemporaneous cohort stays unchanged; observe through specified settling and measurement windows; compare within matched load and traffic strata; after a removal-associated improvement, conditionally reintroduce the same candidate within safety thresholds and observe again under comparable conditions. If load cannot be adequately matched in production, controlled representative workload replay in staging is used, and that setting is retained as a boundary on the inference.
source_neutral.action: 1. Before any production perturbation, specify: the checkout latency metric; the minimum meaningful response; the traffic strata; the observation duration; the expected propagation and warm-up delays; and the latency, error and resource safety thresholds. 2. Where the candidate is independently reversible and removal is safe, remove the candidate alone from a bounded cohort and keep a comparable contemporaneous cohort unchanged. 3. Hold configuration and capacity stable. Record request arrival rate, request mix, traces and resource metrics in both cohorts. 4. Observe through the specified settling and measurement windows and compare changes within matched load and traffic strata. 5. If load cannot be adequately matched in production, run controlled representative workload replay in staging and carry that setting forward as an inference boundary. 6. After a removal-associated improvement, reintroduce the same candidate if this is justified and within the safety thresholds, then observe under comparable conditions. 7. If any threshold is crossed during reintroduction, stop reintroduction and restore the safer state. 8. If concurrent changes, contamination of the unchanged cohort, or unmatched load defeat the comparison, stop causal interpretation. 9. If reversibility or safety cannot be established, do not perturb production. 10. If removal produces no meaningful response after the specified delay window, do not reintroduce for the sole purpose of provoking degradation; inspect traces and test a competing candidate. 11. If a bundle responds, isolate or bisect its members in staging before attributing the effect to one change.
source_neutral.observables: Signals sought: (a) a meaningful decrease in the checkout latency metric after removal, exceeding the change seen in the contemporaneous unchanged cohort, and occurring within comparable request-rate and request-mix strata; (b) if safe reintroduction occurs, a rise in latency again after the specified settling delay under comparable load. Recorded alongside: timing of the response, effect size, variability, request traces, and resource behavior, plus request arrival rate and request mix in both cohorts. Signals that count as weaker or incomplete evidence instead of the proposed reproducible removal/restoration signal: a latency decrease that coincides with falling load in both cohorts; an inconsistent response; an early stop triggered by a safety threshold.
source_neutral.inferential_warrant: A latency decrease on removal, followed by recurrence on restoration, that is reproducible under comparable workloads and absent from the unchanged cohort increases support for the claim that the tested change contributes causally to checkout latency, within the tested version, configuration, traffic and capacity conditions. This comparison makes load variation alone a less adequate explanation. It does not establish that the change is the sole cause, and it does not establish that the change's effect is independent of load. An improvement observed on removal without a restoration observation supports a more limited attribution. A response at the bundle level supports attribution to the bundle and not to any single member. An adequate negative removal test weakens the candidate hypothesis within the tested conditions, without excluding delayed effects, persistent effects, or load-dependent effects that were not tested. Results obtained from staging replay are bounded by that setting.
source_neutral.problem_decomposition: Units: (1) the candidate deployed change, selected from deployment/configuration history and request traces; (2) the rollback bundle, meaning the candidate plus any other revisions, configuration or shared state that change together with its removal; (3) the affected checkout paths; (4) traffic strata defined by request rate and request mix; (5) the bounded cohort from which the candidate is removed; (6) the comparable contemporaneous cohort left unchanged; (7) the pre-specified parameters: latency metric, minimum meaningful response, observation duration, propagation and warm-up delays, settling and measurement windows, and latency/error/resource safety thresholds; (8) recorded covariates: request arrival rate, request mix, traces, resource metrics; (9) the two test settings, production and staging workload replay; (10) competing candidate changes. Relationships: the tested factor is the single candidate when it is independently reversible and is the whole bundle when it is not separable; the changed cohort is compared against the unchanged cohort within matched load and traffic strata so that the effect of the change is separated from the effect of load variation; removal and reintroduction are sequential phases applied to the same candidate, with reintroduction conditional on a removal-associated improvement, justification and safety thresholds; hypotheses about causal role, reversibility and safety are checked separately; bundle-level responses are decomposed into members through isolation or bisection in staging; a response confined to particular load strata is treated as a possible interaction between the change and load.
source_neutral.next_inquiry: Specified follow-up: (a) if removal produces no meaningful response after the specified delay window, inspect traces and test a competing candidate, without reintroducing for the sole purpose of provoking degradation; (b) if a bundle responds, isolate or bisect its members in staging before attributing the effect to one change; (c) if load cannot be adequately matched in production, use controlled representative workload replay in staging and retain that setting as an inference boundary; (d) after a removal-associated improvement, reintroduce the same candidate if justified within the safety thresholds and observe under comparable conditions. No further follow-up beyond these is specified, including for the case where causal interpretation is stopped or where production perturbation is not performed.
source_neutral.limits: Conditions: production removal is performed where the candidate is independently reversible and removal is safe; reintroduction is performed after a removal-associated improvement and where justified within safety thresholds; comparison requires stable configuration and capacity, a comparable contemporaneous unchanged cohort, and matched load and traffic strata. Stopping rules: stop reintroduction and restore the safer state if any latency, error or resource threshold is crossed; stop causal interpretation if concurrent changes, contamination of the unchanged cohort, or unmatched load defeat the comparison; do not perturb production if reversibility or safety cannot be established; do not reintroduce solely to provoke degradation when removal yields no meaningful response after the specified delay window. Uncertainties and inferential limitations: latency may improve or worsen spontaneously; concurrent deployments, dependency changes, traffic shifts, imperfect cohort matching and shared-resource interference can mimic or obscure a response; queue drainage, caches, asynchronous work and persistent data changes may outlast removal; uncertain settling time makes a negative result inconclusive; a response confined to particular load strata may reflect an interaction between the change and load; reintroduction may be unsafe or impossible; staging replay may omit production behavior; conclusions apply to the tested version, configuration, traffic and capacity conditions; sole causation and load-independence of the effect are not established. These limits constrain attribution even when timing aligns. The procedure does not identify which change is actually responsible without the proposed observations being made.
